title: I Refused to Change the Grade and the Parent Went to the Board
author: Larry J. Walsh
summary: Larry J. Walsh retells, from the principal's chair, a month in which a father pursued two grade points that stood between his son and an eight-thousand-dollar scholarship. The father brought a self-built spreadsheet, argued that the district's extracurricular policy excused late work, and ultimately named Walsh at a school board meeting. Walsh weighed two real arguments, but the teacher had applied her syllabus identically to every student, and four classmates had turned in the same assignments late. He held the grade, then protected the teacher in writing and by calling the superintendent with documentation, which ended the matter in one short call. The boy won a smaller scholarship later, and the teacher stayed eight more years because she had not been left to defend herself alone. Walsh distils the lesson that an exception for the persistent is a penalty on families who did not push, and that leaders must stand with teachers out loud and in writing.
points: A grade changed for one family quietly costs the families who did not push, and they often have the least power to push.
Weigh a parent's argument seriously (here a real policy), but ask whether the teacher applied her published rules the same way to everyone.
Keep documentation ready so a superintendent's two questions, did you follow policy and did you treat the student like everyone else, can be answered before first period.
Protect the teacher publicly and in writing, because she will remember for years whether you stood with her.
Do not over-read a parent's later silence or nod; hold the line and let the relationship settle on its own.
quotes: A grade changed for one family is a grade stolen from another.
A school leader will be asked, over and over, to make a small exception for a family who is persistent enough to ask for it. The exception always looks small from inside the meeting, and it never is.

Every grade, every discipline decision, and every policy you bend for the loudest family becomes a quiet penalty on the families who did not push, and they are often the ones with the least power to push.

Hold the line when the policy is clear and the teacher applied it fairly. Then protect the teacher out loud and in writing, because the parent’s anger will pass, but the teacher will remember for years whether you stood with her when it mattered.

The father had a real argument. The district’s extracurricular policy said students should not be penalized for school-sanctioned events. The tournament was school-sanctioned. (He had printed that policy too.)
The teacher had a real argument. The policy covered work due on the day of the event, not work due two weeks before it. She had followed her syllabus exactly, the same way for every student.
He asked two questions. Did I follow the policy? Did I treat the student the same as everyone else in the class? I said yes to both and emailed him the documentation before first period.

The teacher stayed eight more years. She told me once in passing that the board meeting was the moment she decided she would not leave. Not because of what the father said but because nobody made her defend herself alone.
